reviews.author: CinemaSerf
reviews.content: It was always going to be very difficult for this to hold a candle to “Kind Hearts and Coronets” (1949) but I wasn’t really prepared for something quite this insubstantial. It’s really only a vehicle for the ever-amiable Glen Powell but even his character is disappointingly undercooked and it’s another of these films where it’s best bits featured in the trailers. It’s told by way of a confession between “Becket” and a priest as he awaits imminent hanging. His revelations reveal that his mother was from very wealthy stock, but was abandoned after she insisted in having a child with an wholly unsuitable musician. Left to their own devices, they struggled along until she prematurely died and left him looking for retribution. To pay his bills, he has a job in a tailor’s shop where he encounters his rather snobbish childhood friend “Julia” (Margaret Qualley) who plants a devious seed in his mind. What better way to inherit than to ensure that the seven folks further up the family tree all come tumbling down? With things all going swimmingly, he meets the girlfriend of one of his doomed relatives, “Ruth” (Jessica Henwick) and is soon all loved-up. Thing is, the unhappily wed “Julia” cottons on to his cunning plan and so now “Becket” has lots of plates to spin as he tries to keep the girl, get the Rolls Royce and avoid the drop. There are a few moments that raise a smile, but for the most part the drama doesn’t really catch fire. Part of the problem is that it simply doesn’t develop the roles of the “victims” at all. Each get a few moments in the sun, but their parts needed beefing up much more to enhance the comedic and quirky effects of this dark comedy thriller. Ed Harris bowls along towards the end, but that made little sense and I half expected Tim Curry to emerge from behind one of the wooden panels that line the hallway. Qualley looks the part but her persona has none of the mischievous charm nor scheming intricacy it needed to resonate and I left with a worrying sensation that someone, somewhere, fancies the idea of a sequel should this take the money at the box office. It’s watchable enough, but is another cinematic example of something originally unbroken an in no need of fixing seventy-five years later.

aiEnrichment.summary_one_sentence: Disowned at birth by his obscenely wealthy family, a working-class man schemes to reclaim his multi-billion-dollar inheritance by systematically eliminating every relative standing in his way.
aiEnrichment.summary_short: Raised in modest circumstances after his mother was disowned by the ultra-wealthy Redfellow family, Becket Redfellow reaches a breaking point in his working-class life. Fueled by a desire to honor his late mother and secure a massive fortune, he devises a dark plan to systematically murder the estranged relatives standing between him and the estate. Balancing his escalating spree with a high-stakes corporate entry and complicated personal relationships, Becket rapidly descends into a web of deceit. Ultimately, his quest for vengeance forces him to confront the dark, blood-stained reality of extreme wealth.
aiEnrichment.summary_long: How to Make a Killing follows Becket Redfellow, a blue-collar worker raised in Newark after his mother was cast out by the ultra-wealthy Redfellow dynasty. After losing his job and remembering his mother's deathbed wish to reclaim what is rightfully theirs, Becket realizes he is in line to inherit a multi-billion-dollar estate. Determined to claim the fortune, he launches a calculated campaign to eliminate his entitled cousins and relatives one by one through seemingly accidental deaths. Along the way, he secures a job at his unsuspecting uncle's firm and begins falling in love with Ruth, a grounded teacher who offers him a path to a quiet life. However, the re-emergence of his manipulative childhood crush Julia and his own growing obsession with vengeance push him further into his dark enterprise. Becket continues orchestrating elaborate homicides, targeting a playboy stockbroker, a bohemian artist, a hypocritical megachurch pastor, and a self-serving philanthropist. As his corporate influence grows alongside his body count, Becket finds it increasingly impossible to walk away from the fortune. His murderous spree eventually brings him face-to-face with the family's ruthless patriarch, Whitelaw Redfellow, who demands a final test of loyalty. Trapped between his genuine feelings for Ruth and his insatiable drive for revenge, Becket's carefully constructed secret life begins to unravel. Ultimately, his relentless crusade forces him to face the true cost of entering the cutthroat Redfellow legacy.
aiEnrichment.synopsis: How to Make a Killing is a darkly comedic thriller centered on Becket Redfellow, a young working-class man who grew up in modest circumstances after his mother was disowned by her exceptionally wealthy family. Upon facing career setbacks and reflecting on his late mother's final wish, Becket discovers that he remains in line to inherit the multi-billion-dollar Redfellow estate if the relatives ahead of him were to pass away. Motivated by a desire for class retribution and financial freedom, Becket embarks on a calculated quest to eliminate the entitled heirs standing in his way, disguising his deeds as tragic misfortunes while infiltrating the inner sanctums of corporate high society. As he balances his lethal ambition with new professional opportunities and personal relationships, Becket must navigate the dangerous complexities of greed, morality, and family legacy.

story_structure.resolution: Becket faces the fallout of his ruthless crusade, grappling with legal entanglements and the ultimate price of pursuing wealth through betrayal.
story_structure.introduction: Becket Redfellow grows up as a working-class outsider after his mother is disowned by her ultra-wealthy family, leaving him carrying the desire to reclaim his rightful place in high society.
story_structure.risingAction: Becket launches a calculated scheme to systematically eliminate his relatives, balancing his dark ambitions against growing FBI scrutiny, newfound romance, and corporate advancement.
